Storm Preparation & Tree Safety Checklist for NE Ohio Homeowners

Severe-storm season in NE Ohio runs roughly April through October, with a secondary winter ice-storm peak. Most of the worst tree damage is preventable with a 30–60 minute walk-around before the season starts — here is exactly what to look for and what to do if a tree does come down.

We would rather flag a problem tree in April than extract one from your roof in July. This checklist walks through pre-season inspection, the wind-risk signs that matter, and what to do in the first 24 hours after a storm. Print it, walk your property, and call {{global.phone}} if anything you find concerns you — Roubic hazard assessments are free.

Pre-Season Tree Inspection — Walk Your Property

Walk every tree taller than 20 ft within striking distance of your house, garage, fence, pool, or driveway. Striking distance roughly equals tree height — a 60-foot tree should be inspected if it stands within 60 feet of a target. Here is what to check on each one:

  1. Trunk cracks or splits — vertical splits that run into the wood, not just the bark, are structural failure points.
  2. Fungal conks at the base — mushrooms growing from the trunk or root flare indicate active wood decay. Photograph and call for assessment.
  3. Sudden lean — a tree that looks more leaned than last year often means root-plate failure has begun.
  4. Soil heaving or cracking — on the high side of any leaning trunk, this is the visible signal of root-plate movement.
  5. Large dead branches over targets — deadwood drops unpredictably; schedule removal before storm season.
  6. Co-dominant leaders (V-shaped forks) — with included bark between them, these fail in wind events. Cabling or selective removal extends the tree's life.
  7. Ash trees — D-shaped exit holes, bark splits, and woodpecker damage signal emerald ash borer. EAB-killed ash turn brittle and fail violently, usually within 18–24 months of full canopy loss.
  8. Oak trees — outside-in browning leaves, rapid leaf drop, and top-down decline can mean oak wilt; the tree may fail by the next storm season.
  9. Photograph anything concerning — capture angle, distance, and a date stamp for insurance baselines and hazard-assessment calls.

Specific Wind-Risk Signs

Some defects are worse than others. These are the signs Aaron weights most heavily when judging whether a tree will survive the next significant wind event:

  1. Sudden new lean over 15° — HIGH. Root-plate has likely failed; the tree will come down in the next significant wind.
  2. Vertical trunk crack into the wood — HIGH. Structural integrity is already compromised; storm wind completes the failure.
  3. Decay or hollow at a structural junction — HIGH. Junction points fail catastrophically when decayed.
  4. EAB-killed ash within striking distance — HIGH. Brittle wood produces "widow-makers" that fail without warning.
  5. Heavy, one-sided or asymmetric crown — MEDIUM. Wind load is unevenly distributed and failure often occurs on the heavy side.
  6. Co-dominant leaders with included bark — MEDIUM. A common storm-failure mode — the V splits open under wind load.
  7. Large dead branches over targets — MEDIUM. Deadwood drops first in storms and can damage structures or vehicles below.
  8. Power-line proximity — VARIES. Coordinate with the utility; never work near energized lines.

Post-Storm — The First 24 Hours

If a storm has already hit, work through these steps in order. Safety first, documentation second, cleanup last.

  1. Confirm everyone is safe before going outside. Lightning can strike up to 30 minutes after the visible storm passes — if you can hear thunder, stay indoors.
  2. Stay away from any tree on a power line. Assume every downed line is energized. Call the utility first and do not touch anything contacting the line.
  3. Do not approach a leaning or partially-fallen tree. Spring tension in trapped wood can release violently — storm-damaged trees are the leading cause of tree-related fatalities nationally.
  4. Photograph everything before cleanup begins. Wide shots of the full scene, close-ups of impact points, and model or serial numbers if vehicles or equipment were damaged.
  5. Tarp any structural breach. If a tree opened a hole in your roof, water damage over the next day often exceeds the original tree damage. Tarping is fast triage; the real repair comes later.
  6. Call your insurance company's claims line. Open the claim within 24 hours if possible with your policy number and the date and time of damage. Note the claim number for every follow-up call.
  7. Call Roubic's emergency line for extraction. {{global.phone}}. We respond within 2–4 hours for tree-on-structure events in our primary service area and provide insurance documentation as part of the workflow.
  8. Walk the rest of the property for additional hazards. After one tree fails, others nearby may have hidden damage — partial uprooting, hung branches, and crowns that lost large limbs.

Storm Damage & Homeowners Insurance

Homeowners insurance generally covers storm-damage tree removal when a tree damages a covered structure — house, garage, certain fences, and a vehicle in some scenarios. It typically does not cover removal of a tree that fell without damaging anything, or routine removal of a healthy tree. Roubic builds the documentation your carrier needs — photos, itemized work, species and diameter estimates — directly into the storm-response workflow so the claim moves through cleanly.

Bottom Line — Aaron's Advice

Removing every tree out of storm anxiety is not a sound strategy. Healthy mature trees survive routine storms and actually buffer wind and protect property. The right approach is an annual hazard assessment that flags the trees with real structural risk and leaves the healthy canopy in place.

The cheapest quote isn't usually the safest. Look at the line items, not just the total — a quote without insurance documentation, a written method, or a cleanup scope is hiding something, usually the parts that protect you. {{global.owner_name}} · Owner

Common Storm-Prep Questions

Storm Preparation FAQ

How do I prepare my trees for storm season?
Walk your property in spring before severe-storm season starts. Inspect every mature tree within striking distance (roughly tree height) of your house, garage, fence, pool, or driveway. Look for sudden lean, vertical trunk cracks, fungal conks at the base, large dead branches over targets, co-dominant leaders, and disease symptoms — EAB on ash, oak wilt on oak. Schedule pruning or removal for anything structurally compromised. That 30–60 minute walk-around in April prevents most preventable storm damage.
What should I do if a tree falls on my house?
Make sure everyone is safe and stay away from the tree until you have checked for power lines. Photograph everything before cleanup starts, then tarp any roof breach to prevent water intrusion. Call your homeowners insurance claims line within 24 hours, and call Roubic's emergency line at {{global.phone}} for extraction. Do not attempt DIY removal — storm-damaged trees have unpredictable spring tension and are the leading cause of tree-related fatalities nationally.
Does homeowners insurance cover storm-damage tree removal?
Generally yes, when a tree damages a covered structure — house, garage, certain fences, or a vehicle in some scenarios. Insurance typically does not cover removal of a tree that fell without damaging anything, or routine removal of a healthy tree. Roubic provides the documentation carriers want — photos, itemized work, species and diameter estimates — built into the storm-response workflow so your claim moves through cleanly.
How quickly can Roubic respond to a storm emergency?
We aim to be on-site within 2–4 hours for emergencies inside our primary service area — Auburn Township, Pepper Pike, Chagrin Falls, Moreland Hills, Solon, and the surrounding inner-ring suburbs. After-hours and weekend response carries a 50% surcharge over scheduled rates. Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets receive priority but may have slightly longer mobilization.
What is the most common tree-storm-failure mode in NE Ohio?
EAB-killed ash failing without visible warning is the most common single failure mode in NE Ohio right now — brittle dead wood snaps in even moderate winds. After that, co-dominant leaders splitting at the V, followed by root-plate failure on shallow-rooted species like silver maple, willow, and Norway maple on saturated ground. Pre-season inspection catches all three categories.
